title: Silas and the Hymn
premise: When Marguerite Halloran returns to the decaying town of Vesper's Bend to bury their twin sister, they discover the body was never identified—and the funeral home insists it isn't the twin at all. Haunted by sleep recordings that capture a second voice answering questions in Marguerite's own cadence, they uncover the town's founding sin: in 1974, the Halloran family took a house, a name, and a child that belonged to the last resident of Blackwater Row. As the final living witness prepares to sign away her claim, the voice grows bolder, and Marguerite realizes the inheritance was never money—it was a debt. To survive, Marguerite must publicly return what was stolen, dissolving their own family's legitimacy and finding, in the ruin of that confession, the belonging they'd always faked. The book ends with the papers unsigned, the house surrendered, and the second voice finally falling silent—leaving Marguerite alone, documented, and free.
about_author: Elodie Fairweather is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing depositions in small-town probate disputes before turning to horror. They live in a converted funeral home in upstate New York and still keep meticulous records of everything.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives in Vesper's Bend to identify and bury their twin, Colette, but the funeral director's ledger describes a woman with different scars. Marguerite's POV; the beat is cold, procedural dread—the first crack in the story they've been told. They begin photographing documents 'because documentation is a kind of prayer.'

chapters.title: Probate and Ashes
chapters.summary: At the will reading, Marguerite learns the estate passes only if the death is certified, and certification requires a body no one will confirm. Aunt Delphine warns them to sign and leave. Marguerite's POV; the emotional beat is the ache of grieving someone who may not be dead.

chapters.title: Recorder, Night One
chapters.summary: Unable to sleep in Colette's room, Marguerite leaves a voice recorder running and captures a second voice—lower, patient—answering questions Marguerite never asked aloud. Marguerite's POV; the beat shifts from grief to terror as the voice says their childhood nickname, one only Colette knew.

chapters.title: Blackwater Row
chapters.summary: Marguerite investigates the address on an old deed and finds a collapsed street the town maps no longer acknowledge. An elderly neighbor, Ruth Amos, slams her door at the name 'Halloran.' Marguerite's POV; the beat is the first hint that their family name carries a debt.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Marguerite finds the 1974 transfer: the Hallorans acquired the Blackwater house and, with it, guardianship of a child named Odile Vesper, whose records end mid-page. Marguerite's POV; the beat is the vertigo of realizing the family story has a hole shaped like a person.

chapters.title: The Second Voice, Interviewed
chapters.summary: Marguerite begins deliberately asking questions before sleep and recording the answers. The voice describes 1974 in first person: the house, the taking, the child. Marguerite's POV; the beat is compulsion—the horror of needing the voice, of treating it as a witness rather than a threat.

chapters.title: Delphine's Denial
chapters.summary: Marguerite confronts Aunt Delphine with the deed. Delphine burns a box of papers in the sink and orders Marguerite off the property. Delphine's POV; the beat is fear disguised as fury—she has heard the voice before, decades ago, and signed something to make it stop.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Marguerite finds Odile Vesper alive, ninety-one, in a care facility, days from signing her remaining claim over to a development company—papers Delphine helped arrange. Marguerite's POV; the beat is recognition: Odile has Colette's exact scar. The body in the casket was never their twin.

chapters.title: Twin Studies
chapters.summary: Marguerite digs into Colette's last months: her calls, her visits to Odile, her discovery of the same deed. Colette was closing in on the truth when she vanished. Marguerite's POV; the beat is guilt sharpened into purpose—Colette died for the documentation Marguerite is now continuing.

chapters.title: The House Answers
chapters.summary: Marguerite breaks into the derelict Blackwater house and finds rooms preserved mid-life: a child's shoes, a stopped clock, a wall of names. The recorder fills with overlapping voices. Marguerite's POV; the beat is awe curdling into violation—the house has been waiting to be entered.

chapters.title: Ruth Amos, Witness
chapters.summary: Ruth finally speaks: she was a girl in 1974 and saw the Hallorans carry Odile's mother out of the house during the flood that 'took' her. No one was ever charged. Ruth's POV; the beat is the weight of fifty years of silence and the relief of confession.

chapters.title: The Voice Names Itself
chapters.summary: The night voice stops answering and starts asking. It asks Marguerite to say its name. Marguerite, cross-referencing recordings with parish records, finds it: Odile's mother, Marion. Marguerite's POV; the beat is the terrible intimacy of being known by the dead.

chapters.title: Papers, Unsigned
chapters.summary: The development company accelerates the signing; Odile's claim expires in nine days. Marguerite petitions to intervene as kin, and the court laughs them out. Marguerite's POV; the beat is the theme made flesh: the law has no room for this justice.

chapters.title: Delphine Breaks
chapters.summary: Delphine, haunted by recordings Marguerite mailed her, confesses: in 1974 the family took the house legally and the child informally, and every Halloran since has heard the voice and paid to silence it. Delphine's POV; the beat is collapse—the relief and shame of a fifty-year secret ending.

chapters.title: Where Colette Went
chapters.summary: Following the voice's directions, Marguerite finds Colette's car submerged in the old flood channel behind Blackwater Row, and with it her notebook: she'd planned to return the house to Odile the week she died. Marguerite's POV; the beat is grief transmuted into inheritance—Colette left her the work, not just the name.

chapters.title: The Company Men
chapters.summary: The development company's fixers begin following Marguerite, then break into the motel room and steal the recordings. But Marguerite kept copies, documented, notarized, mailed. Marguerite's POV; the beat is defiance—the realization that the archive itself is a weapon no one can burn completely.

chapters.title: Nine Days to Three
chapters.summary: Marguerite goes public: a local paper story, the deed, Odile's photograph, the flood. The town splits—some deny, some remember, some bring their own family's stolen paper to Marguerite's door. Marguerite's POV; the beat is belonging found sideways: the town's silenced finally assembling.

chapters.title: The Night of Questions
chapters.summary: The voice grows desperate as the signing nears; the house begins answering back in Marguerite's own voice, recordings playing in empty rooms across town. Marguerite understands the deadline isn't legal—it's the house itself running out of patience. Marguerite's POV; the beat is escalating dread as the supernatural and legal clocks converge.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Marguerite brings Odile to Blackwater Row instead of the lawyer's office, and the house shows her everything: her childhood, her mother, the taking. Odile refuses to sign the company's papers and, with a shaking hand, accepts the return of the deed instead. Marguerite's POV; the beat is the climax's first resolution—justice done outside the law, witnessed.

chapters.title: What the House Wanted
chapters.summary: The company's men arrive to force the signing and find the house unyielding—doors that won't open, a flood channel that has moved. What follows is never fully documented; Marguerite's recorder captures only the sound of many voices receding. Marguerite's POV; the beat is horror at the price paid and relief that it wasn't theirs.

chapters.title: Silence, Documented
chapters.summary: The voice stops. Marguerite records forty nights of nothing and files the recordings in the county archive beside the corrected deed. Colette's body is finally identified and buried under her own name. Marguerite's POV; the beat is mourning completed at last—grief given its proper paperwork.

chapters.title: The Hymn
chapters.summary: Marguerite stays in Vesper's Bend, helping Odile restore the house and the town's erased records. On the last page, Marguerite sings the hymn Marion Vesper once sang to her children—the one the voice had been trying to remember—and the house, for the first time, feels like home to someone. Marguerite's POV; the beat is belonging earned through return: the inheritance was never the house, but the obligation to make things right.
